name: Protein intake for hair
lead: Protein intake for hair is the idea that eating enough protein keeps hair growing well and looking thick, because hair is made largely of keratin. People focus on it as part of a nutrition approach to fuller, healthier-looking hair, and it comes up in hair and looksmaxxing discussions alongside iron, zinc and other nutrients.

Keratin is the main structural material of hair, and Wikipedia reports that human hair is roughly 14 percent cysteine, the sulfur-containing amino acid that forms the cross-links giving keratin its strength [3]. Hair-care references state that a balanced diet matters and that deficiencies often show first in hair, naming protein, iron, zinc, biotin and other nutrients as linked to dryness, shedding or weak hair, though much of that text is uncited [1].

Dermatology references list malnutrition, vitamin B12 deficiency and iron deficiency among causes of non-scarring hair loss, and state that supplements are not typically recommended for hair loss and that there is no evidence for biotin [2]. A 2017 review of diet and hair loss recommended screening people with hair loss for risk of nutrient deficiency, correcting confirmed deficiencies, and noted that evidence does not yet show whether supplements help people without a documented deficiency [4]. No trial has tested extra protein for hair in people whose intake is already adequate.
infobox: Hair is composed mainly of keratin protein

paras: Hair keratins are alpha-keratins, coiled helices cross-linked by disulfide bonds between cysteine residues, which makes hair strong and flexible [3]. The body builds this protein from dietary amino acids, which is the basis of the claim that protein intake supports hair.

sections.h: Reported links between nutrition and hair
paras: Hair-care references say deficiencies of nutrients including protein can appear in the hair, and that growth is about 1.25 cm per month.[1] Hair-loss references mention malnutrition and iron or B12 deficiency as less common non-scarring causes.[2]

Wikipedia lists eating disorders and crash diets among possible triggers of telogen effluvium, a diffuse shedding that can appear about two to three months after follicles are pushed prematurely into the resting phase [5].

A hair-loss reference says supplements are not typically recommended, and that for most alternative remedies evidence is insufficient.[2] The 2017 diet and hair loss review likewise reported that evidence does not yet show benefit from supplements in people without a documented deficiency, and that some supplements may worsen hair loss or cause toxicity [4].
No studies found testing higher protein intake for hair in people with adequate intake. Related research is a 2017 review of nutrient deficiency and supplement use in hair loss [4].

card.summary: Eating enough protein for hair; deficiency links are noted, but no trials test extra protein.
card.note: References link deficiency, not extra intake, to hair changes.

quick.overview:
The idea is that because hair is keratin, adequate dietary protein supports hair. References note deficiencies can show up in hair.

No studies were found testing extra protein for hair in people with normal intake.
quick.mechanism: Hair is made of keratin protein, so growth is thought to depend on adequate nutrition.
quick.risks: References do not report specific harms; hair-loss references note evidence for supplements is insufficient, and deficiencies like iron or B12 are cited as causes of hair loss.

chain: Adequate dietary protein supplies amino acids such as cysteine
Follicles have the raw material to build keratin hair
Hair can grow and hold density rather than thinning from shortfall
angle.text: People eat enough protein so the follicles are not short of building material, aiming to keep hair growing at its normal rate and density. The link described in references is between deficiency and hair changes.
